claim: The temporal activity of many physical and biological systems exhibits fluctuations simultaneously varying over a large range of timescales.
source: The temporal activity of many physical and biological systems, from complex networks to neural circuits, exhibits fluctuations simultaneously varying over a large range of timescales.
evidence: This is a general statement about physical and biological systems presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Long-tailed distributions of intrinsic timescales have been observed across neurons simultaneously recorded within the same cortical circuit.
source: Long-tailed distributions of intrinsic timescales have been observed across neurons simultaneously recorded within the same cortical circuit.
evidence: This statement refers to experimental observations but does not provide specific citations in this sentence of the abstract.

claim: The mechanisms leading to temporal heterogeneity in neural circuits are yet unknown.
source: The mechanisms leading to this striking temporal heterogeneity are yet unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Neural circuits endowed with heterogeneous neural assemblies of different sizes naturally generate multiple timescales of activity spanning several orders of magnitude.
source: Here, we show that neural circuits, endowed with heterogeneous neural assemblies of different sizes, naturally generate multiple timescales of activity spanning several orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Neural timescales depend on assembly size.
source: We develop an analytical theory using rate networks, supported by simulations of spiking networks with cell-type specific connectivity, to explain how neural timescales depend on assembly size
evidence: This is a theoretical result supported by analytical theory and simulations.

claim: The model can naturally explain the long-tailed timescale distribution observed in the awake primate cortex.
source: show that our model can naturally explain the long-tailed timescale distribution observed in the awake primate cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Large assemblies preferentially entrain slow spectral components of broadband input.
source: we found that large and small assemblies preferentially entrain slow and fast spectral components of the input, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from driving recurrent networks with time-dependent input.

claim: Small assemblies preferentially entrain fast spectral components of broadband input.
source: we found that large and small assemblies preferentially entrain slow and fast spectral components of the input, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from driving recurrent networks with time-dependent input.

claim: Heterogeneous assemblies can provide a biologically plausible mechanism for neural circuits to demix complex temporal input signals.
source: Our results suggest that heterogeneous assemblies can provide a biologically plausible mechanism for neural circuits to demix complex temporal input signals by transforming temporal into spatial neural codes via frequency-selective neural assemblies.
evidence: This is an interpretation and suggestion based on the results of the study.

claim: Spin glasses exhibit aging and relaxation effects whose timescales span several orders of magnitude.
source: In condensed matter physics, spin glasses typically exhibit aging and relaxation effects whose timescales span several orders of magnitude (Bouchaud, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bouchaud, 1992.

claim: Metabolic networks of E. coli generate fluxes with a power-law distribution of rates.
source: In biological systems, metabolic networks of E. coli generate fluxes with a power-law distribution of rates (Almaas et al., 2004; Emmerling et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Almaas et al., 2004 and Emmerling et al., 2002.

claim: Gas release in yeast cultures exhibits frequency distributions spanning many orders of magnitude.
source: Gas release in yeast cultures exhibits frequency distributions spanning many orders of magnitude (Roussel and Lloyd, 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Roussel and Lloyd, 2007.

claim: Frequency distributions spanning many orders of magnitude endow yeast cultures with robust and flexible responses to the environment.
source: Gas release in yeast cultures exhibits frequency distributions spanning many orders of magnitude (Roussel and Lloyd, 2007), endowing them with robust and flexible responses to the environment (Aon et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aon et al., 2008.

claim: A hierarchy of timescales in the activity of single neurons is observed across different cortical areas from occipital to frontal regions.
source: In the mammalian brain, a hierarchy of timescales in the activity of single neurons is observed across different cortical areas from occipital to frontal regions (Murray et al., 2014; Siegle et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murray et al., 2014; Siegle et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020.

claim: Neurons within the same local circuit exhibit a large range of timescales from milliseconds to minutes.
source: Moreover, neurons within the same local circuit exhibit a large range of timescales from milliseconds to minutes (Bernacchia et al., 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2016; Miri et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernacchia et al., 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2016; Miri et al., 2011.

claim: Heterogeneity of neuronal timescales was observed in awake animals during periods of ongoing activity in the absence of external stimuli or behavioral tasks.
source: This heterogeneity of neuronal timescales was observed in awake animals during periods of ongoing activity in the absence of external stimuli or behavioral tasks
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations.

claim: Long-tailed distributions of intrinsic timescales may be an intrinsic property of recurrent cortical circuits.
source: suggesting that long-tailed distributions of intrinsic timescales may be an intrinsic property of recurrent cortical circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations.

claim: Leveraging computations on multiple timescales is beneficial when performing complex tasks in primates.
source: Recent studies highlighted the benefits of leveraging computations on multiple timescales when performing complex tasks in primates (Iigaya et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iigaya et al., 2019.

claim: Leveraging computations on multiple timescales is beneficial in artificial neural networks.
source: Recent studies highlighted the benefits of leveraging computations on multiple timescales when performing complex tasks in primates (Iigaya et al., 2019) as well as in artificial neural networks (Perez-Nieves et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perez-Nieves et al., 2021.

claim: The neural mechanisms underlying the emergence of multiple timescales are not yet understood.
source: However, the neural mechanisms underlying the emergence of multiple timescales are not yet understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A heterogeneous distribution of cell assemblies is a common ingredient observed in cortical architecture.
source: The central feature of our model is a heterogeneous distribution of cell assemblies, a common ingredient observed in cortical architecture (Perin et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2019; Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perin et al., 2011 and Marshel et al., 2019, and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Rate networks with heterogeneous assemblies can generate long-tailed distributions of timescales.
source: We first demonstrate that rate networks, whose rate units represent cell-assemblies, can generate long-tailed distributions of timescales when endowed with heterogeneous assemblies (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the study and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The heterogeneity of timescales observed in electrophysiological recordings from awake primate cortex can be explained by the presence of heterogeneous cell assemblies.
source: We then show that the heterogeneity of timescales, observed in electrophysiological recordings from awake primate cortex (Cavanagh et al., 2016), can be explained by the presence of heterogeneous cell assemblies (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in the study by comparing model predictions with experimental data from Cavanagh et al., 2016, as illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: An assembly's intrinsic timescale depends on size.
source: Using methods from statistical physics, we develop an analytical framework explaining how an assembly's intrinsic timescale depends on size
evidence: This is an analytical result derived using methods from statistical physics.

claim: A new chaotic regime emerges where activity is bistable.
source: revealing the emergence of a new chaotic regime where activity is bistable.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical framework developed in the study.

claim: The theory applies to biologically plausible models of cortical circuits based on spiking networks with cell-type specific clustered architectures.
source: We show that our theory applies to biologically plausible models of cortical circuits based on spiking networks with cell-type specific clustered architectures.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations of spiking networks.

claim: In networks with homogeneous assemblies, chaotic activity is suppressed at a single resonant frequency.
source: In networks with homogeneous assemblies, chaotic activity is suppressed at a single resonant frequency (Rajan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rajan et al., 2010.

claim: In heterogeneous networks driven with time-dependent broadband input, chaotic activity is suppressed across multiple frequencies which depend on the assembly's own size.
source: However, when we drive heterogeneous networks with a time-dependent broadband input featuring a superposition of multiple frequencies, we find that the chaotic activity is suppressed across multiple frequencies which depend on the assembly own size.
evidence: This is a finding from the study when driving heterogeneous networks with broadband input.

claim: A reservoir of timescales may be a natural mechanism for cortical circuits to flexibly demix different spectral features of complex time-varying inputs.
source: This spectral specificity suggests that a reservoir of timescales may be a natural mechanism for cortical circuits to flexibly demix different spectral features of complex time-varying inputs.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the spectral specificity observed in the study.

claim: The mechanism may endow neural circuits with the ability to transform temporal neural codes into spatial neural codes via frequency-selective neural assemblies.
source: This mechanism may endow neural circuits with the ability to transform temporal neural codes into spatial neural codes via frequency-selective neural assemblies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential functional implications of the mechanism.

claim: When self-couplings are strong and equal, a third phase appears featuring multiple stable fixed points accompanied by long transient activity.
source: When the self-couplings are strong (order 1) and are all equal, a third phase appears, featuring multiple stable fixed points accompanied by long transient activity (Stern et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2014.

claim: In networks with homogeneous self-couplings, all network units exhibit the same intrinsic timescale.
source: In all these cases, all network units exhibit the same intrinsic timescale, estimated from their autocorrelation function.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of networks with homogeneous self-couplings.

claim: When self-couplings are heterogeneous, a reservoir of multiple timescales emerges.
source: Here, we demonstrate a novel class of recurrent networks, capable of generating temporally heterogeneous activity whose multiple timescales span several orders of magnitude. We show that when the self-couplings are heterogeneous, a reservoir of multiple timescales emerges
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Each unit's intrinsic timescale depends both on its own self-coupling and the network's self-coupling distribution.
source: where each unit's intrinsic timescale depends both on its own self-coupling and the network's self-coupling distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the analytical theory developed in the study.

claim: In a network with a Gaussian distribution of self-couplings in the stable fixed point regime, a complex landscape of stable fixed points emerges.
source: In the case of a Gaussian distribution of self-couplings in the stable fixed point regime, a complex landscape of stable fixed points emerges.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The chaotic phase is characterized by a large range of timescales that can be simultaneously realized across units with different self-couplings.
source: The chaotic phase in the network, Equation 1, is characterized by a large range of timescales that can be simultaneously realized across the units with different self-couplings.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Mean-field theory can generate predictions for rare units with large self-couplings from the tail end of the lognormal distribution.
source: For long-tailed distributions such as the lognormal, mean-field theory can generate predictions for rare units with large self-couplings from the tail end of the distribution by solving Equation 2 and the continuous version of Equation 3, see Methods ('Dynamic mean-field theory with multiple self-couplings') Equation 13.
evidence: This is a theoretical result from mean-field theory.

claim: The solution highlights the exponential relation between a unit's self-coupling and its autocorrelation decay time.
source: The solution highlights the exponential relation between a unit's self-coupling and its autocorrelation decay time (Figure 3aii, purple dashed line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3aii.

claim: During periods of ongoing activity, the distribution of single-cell autocorrelation timescales in primate cortex was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal, ranging from 10 ms to a few seconds.
source: During periods of ongoing activity, the distribution of single-cell autocorrelation timescales in primate cortex was found to be right-skewed and approximately lognormal, ranging from 10 ms to a few seconds (Cavanagh et al., 2016; Figure 3bi).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cavanagh et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 3bi.

claim: A model with a lognormal distribution of self-couplings can generate a long-tailed distribution of timescales which fits the distribution observed in awake primate orbitofrontal cortex.
source: We found that a model with a lognormal distribution of self-couplings can generate a long-tailed distribution of timescales which fits the distribution observed in awake primate orbitofrontal cortex (Figure 3bi).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3bi by comparing model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Neural circuits with heterogeneous assemblies can naturally generate the heterogeneity in intrinsic timescales observed in cortical circuits from awake primates.
source: This result shows that neural circuits with heterogeneous assemblies can naturally generate the heterogeneity in intrinsic timescales observed in cortical circuits from awake primates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Multiple timescales can be robustly generated with specific values, varying over several orders of magnitude.
source: In summary, in our model multiple timescales can be robustly generated with specific values, varying over several orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the analytical theory.

claim: The neural mechanism underlying timescale separation is not an intrinsic property of a single unit but requires the unit to be part of a recurrently connected network.
source: We thus concluded that this neural mechanism is not an intrinsic property of a single unit but requires the unit to be part of a recurrently connected network.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of white noise vs. network-driven dynamics.

claim: The spiking network time-varying activity unfolds through sequences of metastable attractors.
source: The spiking network time-varying activity unfolds through sequences of metastable attractors (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021), characterized by the co-activation of different subsets of neural assemblies (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a and supported by citations to Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012 and Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021.

claim: The dynamics rely on the bistable activity of each assembly, switching between high and low firing rate states.
source: These dynamics rely on the bistable activity of each assembly, switching between high and low firing rate states.
evidence: This is a description of the dynamics in the spiking network.

claim: The dwell time of an assembly in a high-activity state increases with larger sizes and with stronger intra-assembly coupling strength.
source: The dwell time of an assembly in a high-activity state increases with larger sizes and with stronger intra-assembly coupling strength (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The metastable regime in spiking networks is similar to the bi-stable, heterogeneous timescales activity observed in the random neural networks endowed with heterogeneous self-couplings.
source: This metastable regime in spiking networks is similar to the bi-stable, heterogeneous timescales activity observed in the random neural networks endowed with heterogeneous self-couplings.
evidence: This is a comparison between the spiking and rate network models.

claim: In the spiking model, the single neuron current-to-rate transfer function is strictly positive so that the bistable states can have both high and low firing rate values.
source: In the spiking model, the single neuron current-to-rate transfer function is strictly positive so that the bistable states can have both high and low firing rate values.
evidence: This is a description of the spiking network model.

claim: In the spiking network, the rate level depends on the specific network attractor visited within the realization of the complex attractor landscape.
source: As a result, in the spiking network, unlike in the rate network, a variety of firing rate levels can be attained during the high activity epochs, depending on both the assembly size and the the number of other simultaneously active assemblies. In other words, the rate level depends on the specific network attractor visited within the realization of the complex attractor landscape (Mazzucato et al., 2015; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mazzucato et al., 2015 and Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021.

claim: A heterogeneous distribution of assembly sizes yields a heterogeneous distribution of self-couplings.
source: We endowed the network with a heterogeneous distribution of assembly sizes (an additional source of heterogeneity originates from the Erdos-Renyi connectivity), yielding a heterogeneous distribution of self-couplings (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A reservoir of timescales can naturally emerge in biologically plausible spiking models of cortical circuits from a heterogeneous distribution of assembly sizes.
source: We thus concluded that a reservoir of timescales can naturally emerge in biologically plausible spiking models of cortical circuits from a heterogeneous distribution of assembly sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spiking network simulations.

claim: The range of timescales (20 ms-100 s) is consistent with experimental observations.
source: Both the range of timescales (20 ms-100 s) (Cavanagh et al., 2016) and the distribution of assembly sizes (50–100 neurons) (Perin et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2019) are consistent with experimental observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cavanagh et al., 2016.

claim: The distribution of assembly sizes (50–100 neurons) is consistent with experimental observations.
source: Both the range of timescales (20 ms-100 s) (Cavanagh et al., 2016) and the distribution of assembly sizes (50–100 neurons) (Perin et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2019) are consistent with experimental observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perin et al., 2011 and Marshel et al., 2019.

claim: The Schur eigenvectors associated with large positive eigenvalues can be approximately mapped onto E/I cluster pairs.
source: We found that the Schur eigenvectors associated with those large positive eigenvalues can be approximately mapped onto E/I cluster pairs.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the Schur eigenvectors.

claim: Eigenvalues with increasingly larger values correspond to assemblies of increasingly larger sizes.
source: More specifically, eigenvalues with increasingly larger values correspond to assemblies of increasingly larger sizes (Figure 5c), which, in turn, are associated with slower timescales (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5b.

claim: The slow switching dynamics in the spiking network is linked to large positive eigenvalues of the synaptic weight matrix.
source: We conclude that the slow switching dynamics in the spiking network is linked to large positive eigenvalues of the synaptic weight matrix, and the different timescales emerge from a heterogeneous distribution of these eigenvalues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the weight matrix.

claim: In the rate network, the eigenvalue distribution of the weight matrix exhibits a set of eigenvalues with large positive real parts.
source: For comparison, in the chaotic rate network, the eigenvalue distribution of the weight matrix exhibits a set of eigenvalues with large positive real parts as well, Appendix 2—figure 3a.
evidence: This is shown in Appendix 2—figure 3a.

claim: In rate networks, increasingly larger eigenvalues correspond to increasingly larger cluster self-couplings which are associated with slower dynamics.
source: The relation between the value of an eigenvalue and the slow dynamics holds in the rate networks as well: increasingly larger eigenvalues correspond to increasingly larger cluster self-couplings (Appendix 2—figure 3) which are associated with slower dynamics (Figure 3aii).
evidence: This is shown in Appendix 2—figure 3 and Figure 3aii.

claim: In both spiking and rate networks, the reservoir of timescales is associated with the emergence of a heterogeneous distribution of large positive eigenvalues in the weight matrix.
source: In summary, our analysis shows that in both spiking and rate networks the reservoir of timescales is associated with the emergence of a heterogeneous distribution of large positive eigenvalues in the weight matrix.
evidence: This is a summary of the analysis comparing spiking and rate networks.

claim: The correspondence between rate networks and spiking networks should be performed at the level of dynamical modes associated with large positive eigenvalues in the Schur basis.
source: This analysis suggests that the correspondence between rate networks and spiking networks should be performed at the level of dynamical modes associated with these large positive eigenvalues in the Schur basis, where rate units in the rate network can be related to E/I cluster pairs (Schur eigenvectors) in the spiking network.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the analysis of the weight matrices.

claim: In the rate network, transitions are driven by the self-consistent colored noise, the hallmark of the chaotic activity arising from the disorder in the synaptic couplings.
source: In the rate network, transitions are driven by the self-consistent colored noise, the hallmark of the chaotic activity arising from the disorder in the synaptic couplings.
evidence: This is a description of the mechanism in the rate network.

claim: In the spiking network, disorder in the inter-assembly effective couplings may contribute to the state transitions, but there might be finite size effects at play.
source: In the spiking network, although the disorder in the inter-assembly effective couplings may contribute to the state transitions, there might be finite size effects at play, due to the small assembly size.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism in the spiking network.

claim: The phenomenon of stimulus-driven suppression of chaos was preserved when a single rate of adaptation was added to all units.
source: The phenomenon was preserved when a single rate of adaptation was added to all units (Muscinelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Muscinelli et al., 2019.

claim: The sub-population with a slow intrinsic timescale preferentially entrained its activity with slower spectral components of the broadband stimulus.
source: We found that the sub-population with a slow, or fast, intrinsic timescale preferentially entrained its activity with slower, or faster, spectral components of the broadband stimulus, respectively (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The sub-population with a fast intrinsic timescale preferentially entrained its activity with faster spectral components of the broadband stimulus.
source: We found that the sub-population with a slow, or fast, intrinsic timescale preferentially entrained its activity with slower, or faster, spectral components of the broadband stimulus, respectively (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The input amplitude completely suppresses chaos beyond a certain critical value.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the input amplitude completely suppresses chaos beyond a certain critical value, as previously reported in network's with no self-couplings (Rajan et al., 2010) and with adaptation (Muscinelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rajan et al., 2010 and Muscinelli et al., 2019.

claim: The central feature of the model is a heterogeneous distribution of cell assemblies.
source: The central feature of our model is a heterogeneous distribution of cell assemblies, a common ingredient observed in cortical architecture (Perin et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2019; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated as the central feature of the model and supported by citations.

claim: Units are interpreted as neural assemblies consistent with experimental evidence from cortical circuits.
source: In our model, units are interpreted as neural assemblies consistent with experimental evidence from cortical circuits (Perin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Kiani et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014; Marshel et al., 2019), and previous theoretical modeling (Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Wyrick and Mazzucato, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: The neural mechanism underlying the large range of timescales is the heterogeneity in the distribution of self-couplings.
source: We found that the neural mechanism underlying the large range of timescales is the heterogeneity in the distribution of self-couplings (representing neural assembly size).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: This mechanism can be naturally implemented in a biologically plausible model of a neural circuit based on spiking neurons with excitatory/inhibitory cell-type specific connectivity.
source: We showed that this mechanism can be naturally implemented in a biologically plausible model of a neural circuit based on spiking neurons with excitatory/inhibitory cell-type specific connectivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through spiking network simulations.

claim: An assembly's self-coupling represents the strength of the recurrent interactions between neurons belonging to that assembly, proportional to its size.
source: This spiking network represents a microscopic realization of our mechanism where neurons are arranged in assemblies, and an assembly's self-coupling represents the strength of the recurrent interactions between neurons belonging to that assembly, proportional to its size.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spiking network model.

claim: A heterogeneous distribution of assembly sizes generates a reservoir of timescales.
source: A heterogeneous distribution of assembly sizes, in turn, generates a reservoir of timescales.
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network simulations.

claim: The model captured the distribution of intrinsic timescales observed across neurons recorded within the same area in primate cortex.
source: Crucially, our model captured the distribution of intrinsic timescales observed across neurons recorded within the same area in primate cortex (Cavanagh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from Cavanagh et al., 2016.

claim: Comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations across cortical areas revealed a hierarchical structure, varying from 50 ms to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis.
source: Comparison of the population-averaged autocorrelations across cortical areas revealed a hierarchical structure, varying from 50 ms to 350 ms along the occipital-to-frontal axis (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Murray et al., 2014.

claim: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales (from 0.5 s to 50 s) was found across neurons in the oculomotor system of the fish.
source: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales (from 0.5 s to 50 s) was found across neurons in the oculomotor system of the fish (Miri et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Miri et al., 2011.

claim: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales was found in primate brainstem.
source: A heterogeneous distribution of timescales (from 0.5 s to 50 s) was found across neurons in the oculomotor system of the fish (Miri et al., 2011) and primate brainstem (Joshua et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Joshua et al., 2013.

claim: Timescale heterogeneity is conserved across phylogeny.
source: suggesting that timescale heterogeneity is conserved across phylogeny.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations across different species.

claim: Single neuron activity was found to encode long reward memory traces in primate frontal areas over a wide range of timescales up to 10 consecutive trials.
source: Single neuron activity was found to encode long reward memory traces in primate frontal areas over a wide range of timescales up to 10 consecutive trials (Bernacchia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bernacchia et al., 2011.

claim: Autocorrelation timescales were estimated using parametric fits, which may be affected by statistical biases.
source: In these studies, autocorrelation timescales were estimated using parametric fits, which may be affected by statistical biases, although Bayesian generative approaches might overcome this issue (Zeraati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration with a citation to Zeraati et al., 2020.

claim: In the model, timescales were estimated nonparametrically as the half-width at half-maximum of the autocorrelation function.
source: In our model, we estimated timescales nonparametrically as the half-width at half-maximum of the autocorrelation function.
evidence: This is a description of the method used in the study.

claim: In the biologically plausible spiking network model, the distribution of timescales was in the range between 20 ms and 100 s, similar to the range of timescales observed in experiments.
source: In our biologically plausible model based on a spiking network with cell-type specific connectivity, the distribution of timescales was in the range between 20 ms and 100 s, similar to the range of timescales observed in experiments (Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013; Cavanagh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data from multiple citations.

claim: The distribution of assembly sizes in the model is within the range of 50–100 neurons, consistent with the size of functional assemblies experimentally observed in cortical circuits.
source: Moreover, the distribution of assembly sizes in our model is within the range of 50–100 neurons, consistent with the size of functional assemblies experimentally observed in cortical circuits (Perin et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perin et al., 2011 and Marshel et al., 2019.

claim: A fundamental new prediction of the model is the direct relationship between assembly size and its timescale.
source: A fundamental new prediction of our model, to be tested in future experiments, is the direct relationship between assembly size and its timescale.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction of the model.

claim: Previous neural mechanisms for generating multiple timescales of neural activity relied on single-cell bio-physical properties, such as membrane or synaptic time constants.
source: Previous neural mechanisms for generating multiple timescales of neural activity relied on single-cell bio-physical properties, such as membrane or synaptic time constants (Gjorgjieva et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gjorgjieva et al., 2016.

claim: In feedforward networks, developmental changes in single-cell conductance can modulate the timescale of information transmission.
source: In feedforward networks, developmental changes in single-cell conductance can modulate the timescale of information transmission, explaining the transition from slow waves to rapid fluctuations observed in the developing cortex (Gjorgjieva et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gjorgjieva et al., 2014.

claim: Although the average network timescale increased proportionally to the value of the slower time constants, the difference in autocorrelation time between the two populations remained negligible.
source: We found that, although the average network timescale increased proportionally to the value of the slower time constants, the difference in autocorrelation time between the two populations remained negligible.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis in Appendix 3.

claim: Although the heterogeneity in single-cell time constants may affect the dynamics of single neurons in isolation or within feedforward circuits, the presence of strong recurrent dynamics fundamentally alters these single-cell properties in a counterintuitive way.
source: These results suggest that, although the heterogeneity in single-cell time constants may affect the dynamics of single neurons in isolation or within feedforward circuits (Gjorgjieva et al., 2014), the presence of strong recurrent dynamics fundamentally alters these single-cell properties in a counterintuitive way.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with a citation to Gjorgjieva et al., 2014.

claim: A heterogeneity in single-cell time constants may not lead to a diversity of timescales in the presence of recurrent dynamics.
source: Our results suggest that a heterogeneity in single-cell time constants may not lead to a diversity of timescales in the presence of recurrent dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis.

claim: The relationship between an assembly's self-coupling and its timescale relies on the strong recurrent dynamics.
source: Our results further clarified that the relationship between an assembly's self-coupling and its timescale relies on the strong recurrent dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with white noise input.

claim: The mechanism linking the self-coupling to the timescale only emerged when driving the unit with a mean-field whose color was self-consistently obtained from an underlying recurrent network of self-coupled units.
source: Indeed, the mechanism linking the self-coupling to the timescale only emerged when driving the unit with a mean-field whose color was self-consistently obtained from an underlying recurrent network of self-coupled units.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison with white noise input.

claim: A heterogeneity of timescales may emerge from circuit dynamics through a combination of structural heterogeneities and heterogeneous long-range connections arranged along a spatial feedforward gradient.
source: Previous models showed that a heterogeneity of timescales may emerge from circuit dynamics through a combination of structural heterogeneities and heterogeneous long-range connections arranged along a spatial feedforward gradient (Chaudhuri et al., 2014; Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chaudhuri et al., 2014 and Chaudhuri et al., 2015.

claim: These networks can reproduce the population-averaged hierarchy of timescales observed across the cortex in the range of 50–350 ms.
source: These networks can reproduce the population-averaged hierarchy of timescales observed across the cortex in the range of 50–350 ms (Murray et al., 2014; Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murray et al., 2014 and Chaudhuri et al., 2015.

claim: A similar network architecture can also reproduce the heterogeneous relaxation time after a saccade, found in the brainstem oculomotor circuit, in a range between 10–50 s.
source: A similar network architecture can also reproduce the heterogeneous relaxation time after a saccade, found in the brainstem oculomotor circuit (Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013), in a range between 10–50 s (Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miri et al., 2011; Joshua et al., 2013; Inagaki et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2022.

claim: This class of models can explain a timescale separation within a factor of 10, but it is not known whether they can be extended to several orders of magnitude.
